parts.title: THE STORY OF SILK
parts.passageHtml:
The Story of Silk

Silk is a fine, strong, shiny fibre produced by silkworms when making their cocoons. It is thought that the Empress Xi Ling Shi first discovered silk around 2700 BC when a cocoon fell into her cup of tea and unravelled into a long thread. She is said to have developed the silk reel and the silk loom, and arranged for women to be entrusted with the task of silk production.

For many centuries, China kept the secret of silk production, and anyone caught attempting to smuggle silkworm eggs or cocoons out of the country was punished by death. Only royalty and aristocrats were allowed to wear silk garments. Silk eventually became so valuable that it was used as a currency to pay government officials and reward subjects.

The Silk Road, the ancient trade route connecting Asia and Europe, transported silk and other commodities for hundreds of years. Along this route, silk was traded for gold, ivory, glass and wool. Emperor Justinian I is said to have sent monks as spies to discover the silk-production process; they returned with silkworm eggs hidden in hollow canes. This led to the silk industry spreading to the Byzantine Empire around the 6th century AD.

Today, while synthetic fibres have largely replaced silk in everyday use, natural silk remains prized for its unique properties. It is still used in luxury clothing, accessories, and even in medical applications, where its biocompatibility makes it ideal for surgical sutures and tissue engineering.

parts.title: THE PSYCHOLOGY OF COLOUR
parts.passageHtml:
The Psychology of Colour

Colour is one of the most powerful tools in visual communication. Research in environmental psychology has consistently shown that colour significantly influences human mood, behaviour, and decision-making. The effects are both physiological and psychological, with different hues triggering distinct neural and emotional responses.

Red is the most visually stimulating colour. Studies have shown that exposure to red increases heart rate and creates a sense of urgency — which is why it is so widely used in clearance sales and warning signs. In competitive sports, teams wearing red have been shown to win more frequently, possibly because red signals dominance and aggression to opponents.

Blue, by contrast, promotes calm and trust. It is the most popular colour worldwide and is heavily used in corporate branding, particularly in the finance and technology sectors. Research by the University of British Columbia found that blue environments enhance creative performance, while red environments improve accuracy in detail-oriented tasks.

Yellow stimulates mental activity and generates a feeling of warmth and optimism, but overuse can cause visual fatigue. Green, associated with nature and balance, has a restorative effect — hospital studies have shown that patients in rooms with green views recover more quickly than those without. White creates a sense of cleanliness and spaciousness, while black conveys authority and sophistication.

Colour preferences are not universal, however. Cultural context plays a significant role: white is associated with purity in Western cultures but mourning in parts of Asia. Marketers must therefore consider regional colour norms when developing global branding campaigns.

parts.title: URBAN FARMING: FEEDING THE CITIES OF TOMORROW
parts.passageHtml:
Urban Farming: Feeding the Cities of Tomorrow

A. As the world's population continues to shift towards urban areas, cities face unprecedented challenges in food security. Urban farming — the practice of cultivating, processing, and distributing food in or around urban areas — is increasingly seen as part of the solution. It takes many forms, from rooftop gardens and vertical farms to community allotments and hydroponic greenhouses.

B. Vertical farming is among the most technologically advanced forms of urban agriculture. By stacking crops in climate-controlled, artificially lit layers, vertical farms can produce yields up to 100 times greater per square metre than conventional fields. They use up to 95% less water through recirculating systems and can operate year-round regardless of weather. However, the high energy consumption required for lighting and climate control remains a significant obstacle to large-scale adoption.

C. Community gardens represent the opposite end of the spectrum — low-tech, socially oriented spaces where residents grow food collectively. Research has shown that community gardens improve mental health, strengthen neighbourhood bonds, and provide access to fresh produce in so-called 'food deserts' — urban areas where affordable fresh food is scarce. In cities such as Detroit and Havana, community gardens have become vital food sources following economic decline.

D. Hydroponic systems, which grow plants in nutrient-rich water without soil, offer a middle ground. They can be set up in warehouses, shipping containers, or disused industrial buildings, making use of otherwise wasted urban space. Hydroponics typically uses 70–80% less water than soil-based farming and produces harvests more quickly. The main disadvantage is the cost of establishing and maintaining the nutrient delivery systems.

E. Critics argue that urban farming cannot realistically replace conventional agriculture on a meaningful scale. The land area required to feed a city using current urban farming methods would far exceed available space. Proponents counter that urban farming was never intended to replace but to supplement rural agriculture, reduce food miles, and build community resilience. The debate continues, but cities around the world are investing in urban farming infrastructure as part of broader sustainability strategies.
